Join our Team!

We’re 3 Bachelor students from TH Nürnberg (2 Computer Science, 1 Electrical Engineering) with skills in AI/ML, data analysis, software engineering and more!

We have 3 spots left! We’d love to add frontend/web/UI/UX skills, GIS/mapping knowledge, creativity, presentation skills or an interest in space. But everyone with motivation is welcome!

Our project idea will take shape once the detailed challenge descriptions drop on Oct 28.

Curious? We’d love to have you on board!
summary:
ReturnLine is a planning and rehearsal console for one Marswalk to Mount Sharp’s boxwork ridges in Gale crater, explored by NASA’s Curiosity rover in 2025 and 2026. Habitat control directs two suited astronauts from inside the habitat.

It combines USGS image and elevation mosaics from NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and ESA’s Mars Express with Curiosity science sites, images and environmental reference data. Routes use a 1 m terrain grid; a 10 m return-time grid drives a band showing whether the crew can still get home within three limits: 60 minutes to shelter, remaining life support and daylight. The shelter limit draws on NASA’s EVA rescue concept. Return time, slope and daylight can trigger NO-GO; long radio gaps raise warnings. Radiation is background information.

ReturnLine compares routes avoiding protected boxwork terrain with faster alternatives and flags planned crossings of sensitive ground. Crew safety comes first, then planetary protection, then science. A step-by-step rehearsal shows how an injury changes return time, prompts ABORT and brings the crew home. A forearm navigation display and helmet HUD show the crew’s view.

Where can we explore, when must we turn back, and which sensitive ground would our route cross?

Explore Mars. Return Safely. Preserve the Evidence.
details:
The problem

An astronaut on foot needs more than a terrain map: from this slope, at this hour, can we still get home? Walking in a pressure suit is slow, and oxygen and power are limited. NASA’s exploration EVA concept includes getting an incapacitated crew member into a safe haven within 60 minutes. ReturnLine uses a 60-minute walking-time limit as a simplified planning rule; it does not model a complete rescue operation. NASA xEVA concept, §9.2.2

There is a second risk: astronauts carry Earth microbes. Contamination can compromise samples and confuse the interpretation of possible signs of life. This matters at Gale crater, where Curiosity found organic material preserved in ancient rocks. NASA/JPL

What it does

ReturnLine is a planning, navigation and emergency-rehearsal console for habitat control: the crew member inside the habitat who directs two suited astronauts outside. Mission decisions stay with habitat control. The crew displays present the plan; their hardware-style keys change the view.

  • Plan. Habitat control chooses one of four science stops, a planned stay and a start time. The console shows the outward and return legs. The default A* route penalizes protected terrain. A second option, labelled “Fastest route”, removes that protection penalty; the alternative appears faintly for comparison. Finite penalties encourage avoidance but do not guarantee a route without protected-terrain crossings.
  • Check the plan. Four checks cover the outward and return legs: the maximum modeled time to the habitat must be at most 60 minutes; the maximum slope sampled from the 10 m planning grid must be at most 20°; the longest modeled radio gap must be at most 5 minutes; and the crew must return before sunset. The 5-minute radio threshold is our assumption. NASA’s loss-of-communication procedure motivates checking line of sight but does not prescribe that number. NASA xEVA concept, §9.5
  • Read the recommendation. The planner shows GO, GO with constraints, or NO-GO with a reason. Crossing protected terrain can produce GO with constraints when the safety checks pass. The recommendation supports habitat control’s decision. Missing radio data is shown as open; other missing-data cases still need more consistent handling.
  • Watch the return stages. Precomputed walking times determine whether the crew can get home from nearby ground. In this version, green, yellow and red stages appear in a band extending up to 70 m from the displayed routes, alongside a fixed 60-minute contour. The available return time is the minimum of 60 minutes, remaining life support and time until sunset. With the supplied 6-hour life-support setting, the time limit stays at 60 minutes for the first five hours and then decreases. Yellow marks less than 15 minutes to spare. On the crew tablet, the band appears in the “Plain” map view.
  • Rehearse an emergency. “Simulate emergency” presents six steps with explanatory text, manual stepping and auto-play: plan, jump to EVA hour 4:45, reduce the return budget as time advances, continue the return, halve walking speed after an injury, and confirm ABORT to send the crew home. The current data contains no protected-zone polygons, so this rehearsal has no zone drift, reroute or logged zone override. The injured crew still has enough time to get home.
  • Show the crew’s view. A forearm-style navigator offers a heading-up map, hardware-style keys and a data sheet with an elevation profile. A helmet HUD shows home and target bearings, return status and warnings. These are browser simulations of displays intended for use without touch input in pressurized gloves.

The map also includes configurable layers and seven local Curiosity mission place names. Their positions are approximate; they are not official IAU names.

How it works

  • Data prepared offline. Python tools obtain windows of USGS Gale imagery and elevation data using HTTP range requests. GeoMapper aligns the maps and numeric layers. The planning grid has 475 × 476 cells at 10 m spacing. Its elevation samples come from a local 1 m DEM point dataset near the habitat and the 4 m level of the USGS DEM elsewhere, using nearest-point or nearest-pixel sampling. The base orthophoto is displayed at 1 m spacing; an additional 25 cm orthophoto layer covers the local study area.
  • Routes and walking times. Offline A* routing supplies the science routes, including alternatives with and without a protected-terrain penalty. Their walking times are derived from terrain elevation using a normalized Tobler hiking function, with 1.5 km/h on level ground. A separate reverse Dijkstra search computes time to the habitat and next-cell pointers across the planning grid. It uses 16 neighbours, prevents corner cutting past blocked cells, and blocks missing elevation or slopes above 20°. Uphill and downhill times differ.
  • Two protection representations. The A* route alternatives use a boxwork protection mask and report metres inside it. The time-to-base grids and the rehearsal’s zone-entry checks instead use protected-zone polygons. Those polygons are currently absent, so the supplied “zones penalized” and “zones allowed” time-to-base grids are identical. The mask is also available as a map layer.
  • Radio. An offline check estimates line of sight along each planned route and route variant, including Mars curvature. It assumes a 3 m habitat antenna and a 2 m crew antenna. It uses the coarse planning terrain, covers planned routes rather than every possible emergency path, and has no relay model.
  • Daylight. The scenario includes sunrise at 05:47 and sunset at 17:31 LMST, imported from the Curiosity REMS feed for sol 4596. Reusing those historical times for the hypothetical EVA on sol 5120 is an assumption, not a forecast for that EVA.
  • In the browser. JavaScript reads the static files, follows precomputed return pointers, interpolates crew movement and draws the return stages. It performs no route search. Injury changes the walking-time factor. The bundled build can be served locally without an external network connection; the hosted page still needs its files to be loaded.

Source chips explain key displayed values. An assumptions panel lists the walking model, injury factor, life-support budget and other planning parameters.

Safety, protection and science

The intended priority is crew safety, then planetary protection, then science. The planner exposes safety failures and protected-terrain crossings separately. Protection is implemented with finite routing penalties, so even the default route can cross the mask when a target or its approach lies within protected terrain.

The code supports polygon-based proximity warnings, rerouting and zone-entry logging, including an ABORT override. Demonstrating that complete sequence requires consistent protected-zone polygons and a suitable scenario. The current branch does not demonstrate a forced choice between an unsafe protected route and a safe route through a drill-site zone.

What makes it creative

  • Return status is tied to terrain and remaining time, rather than distance alone.
  • Habitat control sees the mission plan alongside the displays the surface crew would use.
  • Protected terrain is visible in route comparisons and planning constraints.
  • The rehearsal makes time pressure and injury consequences explicit, while adapting parts of its explanation to the supplied data.

Factors we considered

  • NASA exploration EVA concepts as the starting point for the planning constraints.
  • Glove use: mission control stays in the habitat, while the simulated crew keys switch display views.
  • Readability: prominent verdicts and status words accompany colour.
  • Traceability: data-derived values and team assumptions should remain distinguishable.
  • One local study area, with explicit limits on what the demonstration establishes.

Honest limits, and what we chose by hand

  • Tobler’s function describes terrestrial hiking. Applying it to suited crews on Mars is unvalidated. Level-ground speed of 1.5 km/h, an injury speed factor of 0.5, and 6 hours of planned life support are assumptions. A further backup hour is displayed but excluded from the planning budget.
  • The habitat location, target selection and rehearsal timing are team choices. Some station descriptions remain generic, and ground-image slots are not filled.
  • The boxwork protection mask is present in the A* routing and map layers. A separate fine-scale ridge-crossing constraint is not included in the time-to-base grid; the console says “ridge mask pending”.
  • The two protection representations are not fully integrated. In particular, the rehearsal cannot log entries into the A* mask through its currently empty polygon dataset. The remaining 80 m buffer parameter is a placeholder, not the geometry of the active mask.
  • With the current rehearsal data, the injured return takes about 7.3 minutes against roughly 54.4 minutes of remaining return budget. Both grid variants give the same result. There is no required protection override.
  • “Fastest route” names the route option without a protection penalty. A* routing costs are not calibrated walking minutes, so this option is not guaranteed to have the shortest Tobler walking time.
  • The radio check can miss small terrain obstructions. Historical REMS daylight values do not establish daylight for the future EVA sol.
  • The Curiosity comparison has not been delivered. Its traverse is loaded from the placeholder dataset, and the header shows “Placeholder data”.
  • Missing shelter-time or slope metrics can currently default to zero in the planning checks. The blanket claim that every unavailable rule remains open would therefore be inaccurate. Some rehearsal labels and summary statements also still need to be brought into line with the data.
  • No astronaut has tested ReturnLine, and nobody, including NASA, endorses it.

Benefits and intended impact

For a crew planner, ReturnLine connects a local route with the time needed to return, terrain constraints and the information shown to the crew. For data teams, GeoMapper and the offline pipeline provide a way to align imagery, elevation and planning layers on a common grid.

Next steps are consistent protection-mask integration across routing and rehearsal, reliable handling of incomplete rule data, a demonstrated safety-versus-protection scenario, daylight for the selected EVA sol, the Curiosity comparison, and walking speeds measured in suited tests. Live crew positions and suit telemetry would be later extensions.

Tools

JavaScript with Vite 7.3.7 and Leaflet 1.9.4 for the static web app, with GitHub Pages deployment configured in the repository. Python with rasterio/GDAL, NumPy, SciPy, pyproj and Pillow for the offline data work, plus the project’s GeoMapper and A* routing modules. Node.js scripts support data checks. Fonts: Atkinson Hyperlegible Next and Mono.

A* routing is connected to the console in this branch. Radiation dose is displayed as information using a fixed reference rate; it is not a safety gate or a local radiation forecast.

Prior research and AI use

Before kickoff, the team selected the challenge and site and researched NASA data sources and EVA concepts. The repository preserves that preparation separately from the implementation developed for the hackathon.

AI coding assistants, including OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude Code, helped produce code and documentation under the team’s direction and review. The repository contains contribution records in docs/ai-log/, and commits include Claude Opus 5.5 co-author credits. These records document AI assistance; they do not independently establish that every contribution was captured.
